Did U.S. officials keep their promises?

ActionOverWords Index (AOW Index) is an independent tracker of specific promises made by elected officials, federal and state, and what actually happened to them: kept, broken, or somewhere in between. Most political coverage tracks what officials say. This tracks what happened to what they said, with every entry linked back to where it came from.

What is tracked

  • 736current officials on the roster, federal and state
  • 29people have promises published on these pages
  • 63promises are published with sources

Every published promise carries sources from at least three distinct publishers, including at least one primary record. Promises still being sourced stay in the interactive tracker, so coverage grows over time.

Federal officials: the President, the Vice President, Cabinet and senior White House officials, a set of sub-Cabinet agency heads, and members of Congress. State officials: governors, lieutenant governors and attorneys general. What is and is not covered.

How it works

  1. One specific promise at a time. Each entry is a specific promise made by an official, with the sources that show what happened to it.
  2. Three sources before a status is set. One official government source, one mainstream/left-leaning news source, and one right-leaning news source. A status only gets applied once it holds up across all three, so it can't rest on reporting from only one side of the aisle.
  3. Six statuses. Not started, In progress, Stalled, Compromise, Completed or Broken, based on what has actually happened, not on intent.
  4. A fixed score. The AOW Score is a 0 to 100 average of an official's tracked promises, weighted by status. The formula is published, so anyone can recompute it.
  5. The same standard for everyone. The same statuses, score and sourcing rules apply to every official, regardless of party.

Corrections

If a status looks wrong, or you want to suggest a promise to track, write to info@action-over-words.com or use the Contact form in the tracker. Appeals need a named source (the outlet and headline being cited), so they can be checked the same way every other entry is. How corrections work.
